planting.note: Plant divisions in spring into moist to wet, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; like the species, this selection spreads aggressively by rhizome in consistently damp ground and is best given room or a contained bed away from choice companions.

directions: Supersize is a Plant Delights Nursery selection of the native sensitive fern, found growing noticeably larger than its neighbors in a wetland population, with broad, deeply cut fronds reaching roughly a yard tall and a reddish central stipe when fronds first emerge in spring. Like the wild species it colonizes moist to wet ground quickly by creeping rhizomes, making it useful for rain gardens, pond edges, or boggy low spots rather than tidy borders. Fronds die back completely at the first hard autumn frost, giving the plant its common name, and the clump re-emerges reliably the following spring. Give it consistently moist to wet soil in full sun to shade; richer, damper soil produces the largest fronds.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring in humus-rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil in shade to bright indirect light; this fern is frost-tender and is best grown in a sheltered, frost-free shade bed in zones 10-11 or as a container/houseplant fern elsewhere.

directions: Tricolor brake fern bears fronds divided into narrow leaflets washed in shifting bands of bronze, pink-red, and green along a dark central stripe, among the most vividly colored foliage of any commonly grown fern. It is widely sold as a shaded bedding plant in the Deep South and Gulf Coast and as a houseplant or terrarium subject farther north, thriving in bright indirect light with high humidity. Keep the soil evenly moist but not waterlogged, since brake ferns have little drought tolerance and will scorch or collapse if allowed to dry out. Protect from temperatures below about 55°F and from direct hot sun, which fades the coloring.

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, acidic soil in partial to full shade sheltered from wind; this Australian tree fern is markedly less cold-hardy than Dicksonia antarctica and needs winter protection or a frost-free site.

directions: Native to cool rainforest gullies of eastern Australia, the bristly tree fern forms slender, often multiple trunks clothed in shaggy brown fibers and topped by a broad crown of finely divided, dark green fronds. It grows noticeably faster than Dicksonia antarctica, adding several inches of trunk a year, but tolerates only light, brief frost and needs shelter from drying wind and hot sun. As trunks age and lengthen they can become top-heavy and topple, so give mature specimens a sheltered, wind-protected position. Keep the fibrous trunk and crown watered regularly, since much of its moisture uptake happens through the trunk surface rather than a conventional root system.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; this East Asian chain fern needs consistent moisture and benefits from a sheltered site at the cooler edge of its range.

directions: Woodwardia prolifera is one of two closely related East Asian species long grown together under the name W. orientalis, bearing broad, glossy, once-pinnate evergreen fronds that can reach several feet long on established clumps. True to its common name, mature fronds often sprout small plantlets directly on the upper leaf surface, which root readily where they touch moist soil to form new plants without division. Give it humus-rich, evenly moist soil and bright shade, protecting the crown in the coldest parts of its hardiness range. It makes a bold textural accent for a warm-temperate shade garden or large container.
sources: Kew Plants of the World Online

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; this extra-large selection needs more room than the typical species and benefits from shelter at the cooler end of its hardiness range.

directions: A Plant Delights Nursery selection of the East Asian chain fern, 'Mama Mia' was chosen for fronds distinctly larger than the typical species, giving an especially bold, architectural clump of glossy, leathery evergreen foliage. Like its parent species it readily produces small plantlets on the frond surface that root where they contact moist soil, making it easy to propagate without disturbing the main clump. Grow in rich, consistently moist, well-drained soil in bright to full shade, sheltering the crown during hard freezes at the cold end of its range. Its outsized scale suits it to a focal spot in a large shaded border rather than a small garden.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial sun to full shade; this evergreen Solomon's seal relative spreads steadily by rhizome into a broad colony over several years.

directions: Disporopsis bakerorum, named for the UK plantsman who first introduced it to cultivation from China, bears upright stems clothed in glossy, evergreen, pointed leaves topped in spring by small, star-shaped white flowers. Established clumps spread gradually by rhizome into a broad, weed-suppressing patch, making it a valued evergreen groundcover for the woodland garden well beyond its native range, including the Pacific Northwest. Grow in humus-rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil in bright to full shade.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring in humus-rich, well-drained, evenly moist soil in partial shade; this frost-tender species needs a frost-free or near frost-free site, or container culture brought under cover for winter outside zones 9b-11.

directions: Despite its common name, pearl orchid is not a true orchid but a shrubby evergreen member of the ancient Chloranthaceae family, grown for small clusters of intensely fragrant, pearl-like greenish-white flowers that in China have traditionally been used to scent tea. It forms a rounded, woody-based clump of glossy, toothed leaves and blooms over an extended period given warmth and humidity. Unlike its hardier, rhizomatous woodland relatives Chloranthus fortunei and C. japonicus, this species is frost-tender and best suited to sheltered shade gardens in the warmest zones or as a container plant moved indoors for winter. Grow in rich, well-drained, evenly moist soil out of harsh midday sun.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; this Korean species spreads steadily by rhizome into a wide-running groundcover over several years.

directions: Green Hankies is a selection of the Korean woodland species Polygonatum involucratum, named for the oddly oversized, leafy green involucre that wraps around each small flower cluster like a tiny handkerchief tucked beneath the arching leaf. The dangling greenish-white flowers themselves are modest, but the bract structure gives the plant an unusual, conversation-piece quality rarely seen among Solomon's seals. It runs by rhizome to form a low, spreading groundcover considerably wider than it is tall, making it useful for filling a shaded woodland bed over time. Grow in evenly moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in dappled to full shade alongside other low woodland perennials.
